item.title: NFL Power Rankings Week 10 Roundup: Chiefs strengthen Top-10 placement
item.description: Let’s see where Kansas City is ranked for Week 10 of the NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
In Week 9 of the 2026 NFL regular season, the Kansas City Chiefs beat up on the New York Jets to advance to 6-2.

Let’s see how the national media reacted to itin this week’s sampling of power rankings:

ESPN: 6

(No change)

Most important game of the second half:Week 12 at the Bills

If the Chiefs want any shot of earning the AFC’s top seed, which would include a first-round bye and home-field advantage in the postseason, they’ll have to go on the road and beat one of their biggest rivals. A win over the Bills on Thanksgiving night would also boost the Chiefs’ odds of passing the Broncos to win the AFC West crown. The Chiefs have played their best this season when at Arrowhead Stadium, averaging 30.0 points per game. — Nate Taylor

The Athletic: 4

(Up from 5)

Midseason grade: A

Sunday was just another example of Patrick Mahomes leaning on Travis Kelce (four catches for 72 yards). The two have now connected for 9,365 yards, surpassing Phillip Rivers and Antonio Gates for the most of any NFL quarterback-tight end pair. The Chiefs may have injuries at wide receiver, but they still rank fourth in the league in EPA per play.

— Chad Graff and Josh Kendall

Pro Football Talk: 6

(Up from 7)

The kicker position shouldn’t be a pick-your-poison proposition.

— Mike Florio

CBSSports.com: 6

(Up from 7)

The defense came alive in a big way against the Jets, getting five sacks. That’s something they will need going forward. The good news was they escaped a possible major injury for Patrick Mahomes.

— Pete Prisco

Yahoo! Sports: 6

(Up from 7)

The most promising part of the Chiefs’ win on Sunday against the Jets might be that Chris Jones and George Karlaftis each had two sacks. Karlaftis had two sacks for the season before Sunday, Jones had just half of a sack, and that’s a big reason the Chiefs’ pass rush ranked near the bottom of the league. Even with five sacks as a team Sunday, Kansas City still has just 14 sacks. That’s the fourth-lowest mark in the NFL.

The Chiefs have been doing fine on defense without much of a pass rush, ranking top 10 in yards and points allowed. But it’s hard to be a top-10 defense while ranking in the bottom five in sacks. Perhaps the performance against the Jets will get the pass rush going, and in turn boost a defense that has already played well.

— Frank Schwab

USA Today: 9

(Up from 10)

It’s easy to miss, but coordinator Steve Spagnuolo’s defense is starting to find a groove − allowing more than 300 yards just once since the Week 5 bye and surrendering more than 20 points just once over the same period.

— Nate Davis

Sports Illustrated: 9

(Up from 12)

I wonder if there was a more wild series of events in a professional football game this year than, right before the half, Patrick Mahomes appearing to have sustained a horrific injury, the Jets squandering the subsequent possession with a missed field goal, Mahomes returning after mere minutes on the sideline and Harrison Butker missing both the initial field goal attempt and the post-penalty field goal attempt. The beautiful game, my friend.

— Conor Orr

Sporting News: 5

(Up from 6)

Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce are up to connecting for 9,360 passing/receiving yards, a new record for a quarterback and tight end combination. Kenneth Walker III is on pace for 24 total TDs and can challenge the single-season franchise record of 27.

— Vinnie Iyer

FOX Sports: 4

(Up from 5)

Patrick Mahomes’ elbow injury gave everybody quite a scare, but the guy is just superhuman, I guess. He got right back in the game and led the Chiefs on a few more touchdown drives in their rout of the Jets, and Andy Reid made it sound like he’s going to be OK in his Monday morning press conference. Obviously, they’re not the same team without him, so his injury needs to be monitored. When healthy, the duo of Mahomes and RB Kenneth Walker is as dangerous as any combo the Chiefs have had during their dynasty. And don’t forget, they’ve got a great chance coming up to prove it in the game they circled on their calendar all along: Thanksgiving night in Buffalo against the Bills.

Stat To Know: Patrick Mahomes improved to 18-0 against teams entering at least four games below .500, extending the best record by a quarterback since 1970 (minimum 15 such starts). 

— Ralph Vacchiano

item.title: Dak Prescott’s deep shot to Ryan Flournoy rescues Dallas
item.description: Ryan Flournoy really saved the day in Indianapolis
item.content:encoded:
Another fourth-quarter lead had disappeared. Another disappointing finish was staring Dallas in the face. Then Dak Prescott and Ryan Flournoy changed the game with one throw.

Trailing Indianapolis 23-20 with 1:37 remaining, the Cowboys opened their final touchdown drive by attacking downfield. Prescott connected with Flournoy for a 46-yard gain, immediately putting Dallas in position to chase the winning touchdown. It was the decisive swing in a much-needed 27-23 victory.

Reaching that point was unnecessarily painful. At halftime, Dallas led 17-7 and later held a commanding 20-10 advantage. However, turnovers and penalties kept Indianapolis alive. Despite moving the ball far more effectively than the Colts, Dallas’s 14 penalties for 153 yards and two fumbles prevented them from converting their advantage into a win. 

Quinnen Williams made a crucial defensive intervention in Dallas territory, forcing Jonathan Taylor to fumble, which Shemar James recovered. However, the offense couldn’t cash in. Indianapolis eventually tied the game, and Brandon Aubrey missed a potential important field goal. Spencer Shrader then kicked a 50-yard field goal with less than two minutes remaining, putting the Colts ahead. 

Dallas needed an immediate response, and Prescott trusted Flournoy to deliver it.

This was no uncontested catch against a defender who had been left behind. Sauce Gardner stayed alongside Flournoy downfield, but failed to turn his head toward the football. Instead, he tried to disrupt the catch through the receiver’s hands and actually grabbed one arm. Flournoy maintained his concentration and secured the pass with the other hand against his body, producing the biggest reception of the afternoon when Dallas needed it most.

The importance of that completion went beyond the yardage. Dallas had started the possession needing to move quickly just to give itself a chance. One snap later, the offense could realistically pursue a touchdown and force Indianapolis to answer. The pressure had shifted straight back onto the Colts.

Dallas finished the job with help from Indianapolis penalties, and Javonte Williams scored from one yard out with 1:08 remaining. The Cowboys had turned a three-point deficit into a four-point lead in just 29 seconds.

There is still plenty to fix. Winning does not erase the mistakes that made this game so difficult. But when Dallas needed a play to prevent another late disappointment, its quarterback and receiver delivered, and the catch was the late-game turning point that helped seal the victory.

item.title: NFL trade deadline 2026: Denver Broncos latest news and rumors

item.content:encoded:
The NFL trade deadline is Tuesday, November 10th at 2 p.m. MT, and our Denver Broncos could be an active team prior to the deadline. They have been widely connected to Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor in the days leading up to the deadline, but according to 9NEWS Denver’s Mike Klis, the team could explore adding a weapon or two to their offense. He mentions running back, tight end, and wide receiver as the positions that they could add.

Looking at the Broncos’ needs heading into the deadline, the most glaring one is running back. Now, the emergence of rookie running back Jonah Coleman helps, but the Broncos still need more from the position. RJ Harvey and Tyler Badie are on the injured reserve, and veteran JK Dobbins has been struggling all season. So, adding another back to pair with Coleman would make sense.

The question is, will they go big and add a Jonathan Taylor or Breece Hall? Or make a smaller move for someone like Tony Pollard or someone else?

Klis mentions wide receiver, and while it may not be the most pressing need right now, it could be in a few months. Jaylen Waddle has not performed as expected thus far; Courtland Sutton will be 32 next season and has a large cap hit(Also restructured his deal and could be off the team next season); Pat Bryant has been very good, but has been on the IR; Marvin Mims is a pending free agent, while Troy Franklin is buried on the depth chart. Could the Broncos be looking to add a wide receiver who could contribute to this team this season and moving forward? This doesn’t seem as likely, but I wouldn’t rule it out if the right deal comes their way.

As for tight end, I don’t know. The only name that could move the needle and that might be available is Dallas Goedert, but is that even worth it? He would certainly improve that room, but the Broncos really do not utilize their tight ends in the passing game. Evan Engram has had a disappointing year, and blocking specialist Nate Adkins leads the group (and, funny enough, the team) in TD receptions with 3, but he only has 6 total catches thus far.

We’ll be tracking all the Broncos news and rumors throughout the weekend and right up to the deadline. It’s supposed to be an active deadline, so we’ll see if our Denver Broncos make any splashes or not in the coming days.

item.title: Falling in love with the Chargers over the summer among Scott Pianowski's biggest fantasy football regrets at midseason
item.description: We all make mistakes. It's important to learn from them. Scott Pianowski goes over his biggest fantasy football regrets.
item.content:encoded:
We’re already into the second half of the fantasy football season, so it’s a good time to do some reflecting on what we’ve missed on. And there will never be any shortage of ideas for a column like this — it’s easier to be wrong than right in this intoxicating, but maddening, game. Thankfully, you only need to be right a little more than the guy next to you to ultimately have a successful season.

It’s been a solid year for most of my teams, as all of my Yahoo clubs have winning records and I’m still alive in my Death League. But today is not a day to play the hits. Now is when we scratch the record, take out the trash, make some sheepish confessions.

Here are some of my 2026 regrets as we move into Week 10.

I didn’t properly rate Kenneth Walker III’s upside

Sure, the frame sounded nice. Walker was stepping into a featured role in Kansas City and leaving the Seattle platoon behind. The Chiefs felt better about their offensive line, too. But it was hard to ignore that Walked was often dinged up with the Seahawks, and had never handled more than 255 carries in a season.

Through nine weeks, Walker is the most impactful fantasy player of the year, rostered on 54.4% of the top-500 Yahoo teams. He’s going to the moon, and it’s frustrating to not be on that ship. I do have a fair amount of Emmett Johnson as a contingency play, not that we ever root for injuries. But if Walker keeps running to fantasy glory, there will probably be cleat marks on my back.

I was mildly skeptical Jaxon Smith-Njigba could be a demigod again

This goes down as a soft fade, because all I did in August was slide Amon-Ra St. Brown ahead of JSN, feeling better about the Detroit infrastructure and schedule. It was fair to wonder if the Seattle offense would drop off without OC Klint Kubiak. Alas, JSN has been just as good as last year, even with Sam Darnold missing some time, and Brian Fleury has been just fine with the play sheet.

Let’s be clear, St. Brown’s WR7 start hasn’t hurt that much. But JSN is two points ahead of the pack on the wide receiver board. It stings.

I stacked some older players on the same teams

This became a long-running joke as I navigated the salary cap draft in my long-standing hometown league. I scooped up perceived values on Derrick Henry ($34), Mike Evans ($5) and Davante Adams ($8), writing “OLD” in the chat log as each offer went final. Any of those players would make sense in a balanced build, but to roster that many back-nine guys on the same team — even if we’re talking about likely Hall of Famers — was probably reckless. Henry (who I’ve since traded) has been in a slow decline this year, Evans is on the injury report every week, and Adams was a forced cut after his hamstring injury.

Normally I would have steered away from this many career-arc concerns, but the offers were so low on Evans and Adams, I couldn’t help myself. I’m feeling the sting of it now, still projected for the playoffs but with no wiggle room.

I didn’t respect Ollie Gordon II enough as a plausible pickup

When De’Von Achane went down in mid-September, every engaged fantasy manager scouted the backfield for a likely successor. I likely paid too much attention to the low returns Gordon showed in limited 2025 action, and not enough eyes on his decent production at Oklahoma State. Gordon hasn’t exactly taken the league by storm, but he’s been the RB19 since the Achane injury, a steady RB2 option. I had the top waiver priority in the Yahoo Expert League when the handoff was made, and my RB2 slot has been sketchy all year. Not selecting Gordon was an unmistakable error.

I didn’t stack anyone with Jordan Love

Even when you get something right, you can pair it with a missed opportunity. Love was one of my favorite late-round QB targets, taking command of a Green Bay offense that can’t run the ball at all. The Packers are the NFL’s most aggressive downfield passing team, and it’s beautiful to watch. But despite my proactive efforts to land Love, I didn’t pair him with breakout receivers Christian Watson or Matthew Golden. Given the simple correlations at play, this feels like an obvious gaffe in retrospect.

I spent a summer in love with the Chargers

We’ll put the most painful one at the end. I believed in new OC Mike McDaniel. I thought they had the offensive line fixed. I saw Justin Herbert as an MVP sleeper, and Ladd McConkey as a perfect fourth-round pick. I even liked the early runout of the schedule, with Arizona in Week 1 and Las Vegas Week 2. Let's do a short-term rental with the D/ST.

It’s all gone horribly wrong. It didn’t help that McConkey was hurt in Week 1 — in the middle of a monster start — and the offensive line quickly fell apart again, but I have to accept that I overrated so many pieces here, especially Herbert and McDaniel. The season can’t end quickly enough for the powerless Chargers. The lucky part of this regret is I didn't get as many Chargers as I wanted in August. Sometimes the football gods save you from yourself. But I have no choice but to own the misguided calls.

item.title: Getting Defensive: Week 10 fantasy plays led by Jaguars, Seahawks; top streaming defenses
item.description: Gary Davenport breaks down the fantasy football defense landscape headed into Week 10 of the 2026 NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
The Jacksonville Jaguars are running away with the AFC South this year, in part due to one of the AFC’s best defenses. For the second season in a row, the Jags are the hardest team in the NFL to run the ball against. No team in the AFC is allowing fewer points per game. The Jaguars are 10th in total defense, lead the AFC with 15 takeaways and are one of four defenses averaging double-digit fantasy points per game.

Jacksonville general manager James Gladstone looked at those numbers and said, “eff those picks.”

The Jaguars didn’t wait for Tuesday’s trade deadline to get better. They were the trade activity Monday, spending big-time draft capital to bring in veteran safety Jessie Bates III and defensive tackle Jordan Davis—the latter of which cost them next-year’s first-round pick.

The Jaguars are all-in on a Super Bowl run this year. Bates is a significant upgrade at deep safety, while Davis should make the NFL’s best run defense that much more impenetrable. And a defense that was already one of the AFC’s best got that much better.

Not bad for a defense that was sitting on the waiver in as many fantasy leagues as not back in the long-ago days of Week 1.

Fantasy Football Waiver Wire Week 10: Corey Kiner and Tank Dell step up
Corey Kiner may have stumbled his way into a starting role on the Patriots, while Tank Dell is finally back in the fantasy picture after a long absence. Both players are strong waiver wire options for Week 10.
  • Kyle Dvorchak,

THE NO-DOUBTERS

Jacksonville Jaguars (at Tennessee Titans)

What? You thought the love-fest was over? Well just like a full-length infomercial, there’s more if you order today! This week the Jaguars travel to face a Tennessee Titans offense that is, um, not good. Only the Philadelphia Eagles are averaging less yards per game this season than the Titans. Tennessee’s 18 points per game is the fifth-fewest in the league. And the Titans are tied for sixth in the league in giveaways. That new-look defense is going to roll in Week 10.

Seattle Seahawks (at Las Vegas Raiders)

It has been a bumpy season for the Seahawks, but the defense has largely held up their end of the deal in 2026—the Seahawks lead the NFL in total defense, rank second against the pass, fourth against the run, fifth in points allowed and seventh among all defenses in fantasy points. A 3-0 start from the Raiders has turned into five losses in their last six games, largely because there just isn’t anything that offense does especially well. Over the last three weeks, the Raiders have surrendered the fifth-most fantasy points per game to defenses.

Kansas City Chiefs (at Atlanta Falcons)

This year’s Chiefs defense looks a lot like most Chiefs defenses under Andy Reid and Steve Spagnuolo. There are a couple big names. A secondary patched together with young players and veteran cast-offs. And all-in-all, a solid unit that ranks eighth in total defense, third in scoring defense and inside the top-10 in fantasy points. Bijan Robinson is a monster at running back, and the Atlanta Falcons have talent on offense. But they also lead the NFC in giveaways and have allowed the third-most fantasy points per game to defenses this year.

Los Angeles Rams (at Arizona Cardinals)

So, um, Myles Garrett is back. Garrett played his second game as a Ram last week and spent most of it in the Commanders backfield, dropping Jayden Daniels three times and forcing a fumble. There are still questions on the Rams defense. But Garrett is back. Aaron Donald is looking more and more like Aaron Donald as he works himself into game shape. And this week the Rams face a Cardinals team with no wide receivers led by a rookie quarterback making his first career start.

Green Bay Packers (vs. Minnesota Vikings)

Jordan Love’s admittedly gonzo passing numbers are the talk of Titletown right now. But a Packers defense that has no Micah Parsons and is short their top-two linebackers is fantasy football’s second-highest scoring defense since Week 4. Safety Evan Williams has played like a Defensive Player of the Year candidate. Despite Parsons’ absence, the Packers are sitting in a tie for fourth in sacks and rank second in takeaways. And this week the Pack hosts a Minnesota Vikings team that was garbage on offense in Buffalo in Week 9.

Pittsburgh Steelers (at Cincinnati Bengals)

It’s understandable that some fantasy managers could have some trepidation about this play, especially if you have watched Joe Burrow making his case as the mid-season MVP over the past month. But the Bengals can’t run the ball with any consistency, and the Steelers are seventh in total defense, fourth in points allowed and third among all defenses in fantasy points. Pittsburgh is also tied for third in sacks with 26, and the key to slowing Burrow down is to get him off his spot.

STREAMERS OF THE WORLD, UNITE!

Baltimore Ravens (vs. Los Angeles Chargers)

The offensive issues in Baltimore (one more starting quarterback and they get a free sandwich) have gotten all the run, but the Ravens have had some defensive issues this season, including just 17 sacks as a team. But the Chargers are a get-right spot for any defense that has 11 players, and this is no exception. The Bolts have well and truly fallen apart. The offensive line is non-existent, allowing eight sacks last week. Justin Herbert looks—broken. And no team is allowing more fantasy points per game to defenses in 2026.

Houston Texans (at Cleveland Browns)

Last week was a make-or-break one from a fantasy perspective for a Texans defense that has mostly disappointed this year, and while there were some lapses once the game got out of hand Houston came through with eight sacks and a pair of takeaways in a win over the Chargers. It’s that pass rush (and arguably the NFL’s best edge-rusher duo in Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter) that’s especially appealing against a Browns team that has given up a whopping 38 sacks in nine games.

New York Giants (vs. Washington Commanders)

The Giants have to be the most surprising first-place team in the NFL. Rookie linebacker Arvell Reese has been a revelation in the Big Apple—the Defensive Rookie of the Year front-runner leads Big Blue in both total tackles (68) and sacks (4.5) after last week’s rampage against the Philadelphia Eagles. The Giants have quietly risen all the way to fifth in fantasy points among defenses, and somehow this team just keeps finding a way through. They will again on Thursday and continue their surprising run.

Buffalo Bills (at New York Jets)

For much of the season, the Bills have won more in spite of their defense than because of it. But Monday night against the Vikings, that defense showed up in a big way, forcing three turnovers, logging a pair of sacks and allowing just six points. This play carries risk with Buffalo on the road off a big win against a Jets team that has shown flashes offensively. But over the past month, Gang Green has been gangrenous, surrendering the fifth-most fantasy points per game.

CAVEAT EMPTOR, FOLKS

Minnesota Vikings (at Green Bay Packers)

To be clear, the Vikings didn’t play poorly last week against the Buffalo Bills, allowing 23 points, taking the ball away once and dropping Josh Allen four times. And the Packers are not going to be able to run the ball on the Vikings the way James Cook and the Bills did. They just won’t. But last week Green Bay walked into Gillette Stadium and absolutely boatraced the New England Patriots through the air, and the Packers sit outside the top-20 in fantasy points per game allowed to defenses.

item.title: NFL Week 10 betting: 5 biggest storylines, including how the Jaguars' trades affected Super Bowl odds
item.description: The Jaguars made some huge moves on Monday before the trade deadline.
item.content:encoded:
Favorites ruled the NFL in Week 9.

Favorites were 14-1 straight up and 11-3-1 against the spread. The week started with the Jacksonville Jaguars easily winning and covering as 10-point favorites at the Baltimore Ravens last Thursday night, and it ended with the Buffalo Bills easily winning and covering as 3-point favorites at the offensively inept Minnesota Vikings on Monday night. It was such a chalky week that only one of 610 remaining entries in Circa Sports' survivor contest was eliminated, according to Yahoo Sports' Ben Fawkes, with a pick on the Falcons.

Here are the top five betting storylines as we head into Week 10 of the NFL season:

Jaguars make a splash

The Jaguars made three trades on Monday, first for safety Jessie Bates III from the Falcons, then for defensive tackle Davon Godchaux from the Saints and a big move for defensive tackle Jordan Davis from the Eagles.

Oddsmakers took note. The Jaguars, already 6-2 and atop the NFL in DVOA and point differential, moved to third in the Super Bowl odds at +750 at BetMGM. They trail only the 49ers and Bills, who are tied for the top spot at +550.

The Jaguars' first test after the trade deadline shouldn't be too tough: They're 10.5-point road favorites against the Titans in Week 10.

A new MVP favorite

With another big game, Joe Burrow has pushed ahead of Josh Allen for the top spot in the MVP odds. Burrow is +200 and Allen is right behind at +225 at BetMGM. Burrow has been on a hot streak and has a favorable schedule in November that gave him a shot at becoming the clear favorite to win the award.

At roughly the midpoint of the season, oddsmakers have the race down to five players: Burrow, Allen, Brock Purdy (+450), Jordan Love (+700) and Trevor Lawrence (+750). Everyone else is 30-to-1 odds or longer at BetMGM. Caleb Williams slipped to 30-to-1 after his four-interception game in Week 9.

Chargers still winless ATS

The Los Angeles Chargers are making a run at history.

The Chargers are 0-7-1 against the spread (or 0-8, depending on the line for a 7-point loss to the Seahawks in Week 4), the only team in the NFL that hasn't had a win for bettors. Every other team in the NFL has covered the spread at least twice, except the Eagles who are 1-8 ATS.

The Chargers are stunningly bad this season and are 5-point underdogs in Week 10 to a Ravens team that will be on its fourth starting quarterback of the season, Jacoby Brissett. At some point the Chargers will cover a spread, but bettors are still waiting for it.

Giants favored on Thursday, and to win NFC East

The New York Giants face a big divisional game on Thursday that can strengthen what is already a tight grip on first place in the NFC East.

The Giants play the Washington Commanders on Thursday night, and they're favored by 2.5 points at home. With the win, they'd be four games up on the Commanders and own the head-to-head tiebreaker. That would leave the Giants and Cowboys as the only two contenders in the division. The Giants are heavy -220 favorites to win the NFC East and those odds would get even shorter if they win to kick off Week 10.

Rams now favored to miss playoffs

The Los Angeles Rams won on Sunday but lost receiver Puka Nacua to a knee injury that will keep him out for a while. That injury, and the depth of the NFC's wild-card race, have made it more likely than not that the Rams miss the playoffs according to oddsmakers.

The "no" for the Rams making the playoffs is at -118 odds at BetMGM. "Yes" is -102. The preseason Super Bowl favorite is in real danger of missing the postseason altogether.

item.title: Jaguars trades for Jessie Bates, Jordan Davis could complicate deadline deals
item.description: It's Let's Make A Deal day in the NFL, with the window on trades closing at 4:00 p.m.
item.content:encoded:
It's Let's Make A Deal day in the NFL, with the window on trades closing at 4:00 p.m. ET. And the deals made on Monday could become a complication.

The Jaguars gave up a lot for two of the three players they acquired. As to safety Jessie Bates III, it was a second-round pick and a fifth-round pick. For defensive tackle Jordan Davis (a run-stopper with 52-percent playing time), it was a first-round pick and a second-round pick.

Those deals will hover over today's talks. Teams that are considering trading players will, at some level, be concerned about the perception that they didn't get enough, relative to what the Jaguars invested on Monday.

If the Jaguars intended that, they're next-level super geniuses. Go all in, acquire players who'll help the team get to the Super Bowl and win it, and make it harder for other contenders to do the same thing today.

As it relates to Jacksonville receiver Brian Thomas Jr., a first-round pick in 2024 who had 1,282 yards as a rookie and doesn't fit the current offense, that could also result in a better haul, if/when the Rams join the effort (which includes the Chiefs, Steelers, and Commanders) to wrest Thomas away from the Jaguars.

Regardless of the motivation(s), Monday's trades by the Jaguars could make it harder for deals to get done on Tuesday. Most notably, it could make the Colts decide not to take the best offer on the table for running back Jonathan Taylor.

With the Giants offering a two and a five, would the Colts be willing to accept for Taylor what the Jaguars gave up for Bates? How much more will it take to get the Colts to believe it's a proper return given the investment made in getting Bates?

However it plays out, if not much happens at the deadline, the wrench thrown into the gears by the Jaguars could be a factor in that.

item.title: 10 Thoughts on the NFL Week 9: The Good, The Bad, and The (Winning) Ugly
item.description: Check out @kdthompson5’s 10 Thoughts on the NFL this week for thoughts on the Bears, Jaguars, Vikings, the Trade deadline, and more!
item.content:encoded:
1. Is it just me, or was there a lot of bad football happening this past week? The Monday night game between the Bills and Vikings, who were absolutely offensive offensively, was just the cherry on top. Maybe it’s just the number of backup/backup-level quarterbacks playing across the league due to injuries and ineptitude. It made teams and quarterbacks who are actually good, like Joe Burrow and Jordan Love, look like they’re playing an entirely different sport. Maybe we should just give everyone a bye week next week.

2. The Vikings are cooked. Brian Flores’ defense is awesome. But even they can’t carry quarterback play this bad for a whole season and postseason. It’s just unrealistic. Eventually, as happened against a persistent Bills offense in the second half, being on the field three-quarters of the game breaks you. Minnesota, to be fair, did try to address their QB situation by signing Kyler Murray. Unfortunately, he’s been hurt a lot and not that effective when on the field. Can’t get worse than what Carson Wentz just did against Buffalo, though. Their defense will win them a few games, but they can’t win their division like this. 

3. Speaking of which…the Chicago Bears now lead the NFC North through nine weeks. Exactly how they drew it up! Slogging through a 2-1 record without Caleb Williams and then winning the ugliest offensive game since the Miracle in the Desert back in 2026? The Bears are back, baby. For real, though: being 7-2, with wins over both of last year’s Super Bowl participants, is a major accomplishment so far for a team many expected to take a step back. The road doesn’t get easier from here, including plenty of games against their divisional opponents (all of whom have six wins or more). But they’re built for it.

4. I don’t know whom the Chargers think they are, exactly. But there need to be a bunch of veteran players not on that team by the time the trade deadline passes this afternoon at 4 p.m. ET. That is a thoroughly uncompetitive, unserious football team, and they should have no delusions about making the playoffs. Follow the Eagles’ example. They just traded defensive tackle Jordan Davis to the Jaguars after trading starting center Cam Jurgens away to the Ravens last month. Khalil Mack, Rashawn Slater, Derwin James. Hell, trade Dicker the Kicker if anyone will send anything for him. Start selling. Now. Otherwise, everyone’s got to get fired immediately.

5. The Jags are getting cooked already for sending a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-rounder to Philly for Davis. That’s a pretty steep price, and that’s coming from a guy whose team just traded two firsts for Jeffery Simmons. Draft capital—the idea of the unknown—is extremely valuable, which Eagles general manager Howie Roseman knows well. When you’re as good as he is at drafting defensive linemen, sending away a good one is no big deal. Here’s what I’ll say in Jacksonville’s defense, though: we as a football community might not be fully appreciating how “premium” a good/great defensive tackle is. But the league seems to be angling in that direction. Great interior defenders make everyone behind them better, meaning you don’t have to allocate as much capital to the positions behind them. Plus, interior pressure on quarterbacks is probably even more devastating than edge pressure. Bottom line: yeah, it’s an overpay. But that doesn’t mean the price isn’t worth it if Davis is even partly what Simmons has been for the Bears so far.

6. Not going to lie, I’m loving the trend of calling horrible, interception-worthy throws “deli meat” or “meatball subs.” I’m not sure if it originated with defensive players, reactor culture, or transitioning from baseball, where throwing one right down the middle to a hitter is a “meatball.” I don’t care. Give whoever came up with this idea a raise, and give Tom Brady a few million more for leaning into it. It’s hilarious.

7. I hope the Eagles start Joe Milton for the rest of the year for the entertainment value alone. Because yeah, this guy is going to struggle to complete the most basic throws (and might accidentally kill one of his receivers with a screen pass). But when it comes to rolling out or chilling way back in the pocket on play-action, the anticipation of wondering how far/how hard he’s about to chuck the ball is intoxicating. Just once, we need him to try to air one out from like his own 25-yard line to the end zone. I bet he could do it. And the Eagles are going absolutely nowhere. So you might as well live with it.

8. For a guy leading a 3-5 football team, C.J. Stroud has been playing some insane ball. He’s on track for easily the best statistical year of his career with 16 touchdowns (his previous season-high is 23) and just two interceptions, and he just dropped 384 yards and five scores on the Chargers with a patchwork-quilt offense around him. The Texans might not do anything this year, unfortunately, especially with the Jaguars running away with the AFC South. But if there’s any argument for still extending Stroud after this season is over, even if they miss the playoffs, this is as good as any. It won’t be what, say, Caleb Williams or Drake Maye is likely to sign in the next few years. But someone’s going to pay Stroud handsomely as long as he keeps this up. 

9. My verdict on the Shedeur Sanders performance, since you’re so interested in it? If I’m grading on a curve, let’s call it “B+,” especially because of the plays he made down the stretch to get the Browns in position to send the game to overtime and eventually challenge for a shot to win it in the end. He definitely outperformed most backups pressed into service this week. But in terms of “representative NFL starting quarterback,” that game is a C at best. Not discounting what he did down the stretch, but even some of the big plays he produced down the field were on underthrown balls his receivers had to adjust to or make incredible catches on. It’s hard to come away thinking anything but, “Thanks for your service, kid. Now sit right back down on that bench.” Again, not bad after that rough first half. But let’s not get ahead of ourselves saying he needs more burn. He really doesn’t.

10. Question for the group: who’s the next head coach to get the axe this season? My hot take: Jim Harbaugh. Because ain’t no way that Chargers team should be this awful. Others, like Aaron Glenn with the Jets or Shane Steichen with the Colts, are playing for teams actively tanking/blowing things up. They know the score. The Harbaugh experiment has run its course, and one more loss might send him. Let us know what you think.

item.title: Vikings QB options include a pair of reunions before NFL trade deadline
item.description: The Vikings clearly have a quarterback problem. Here's a look at the options that make sense for Minnesota before the NFL trade deadline.
item.content:encoded:
The Minnesota Vikingshave a quarterback problem.

It might be one of the league's worst kept secrets, especially since the solution clearly isn't coming from within. The Kyler Murray experiment has failed to this point and the quarterback is now sidelined with a hamstring injury. Carson Wentz put together a clunker on "Monday Night Football" against the Buffalo Bills in what was a dreadful performance.

Quarterbacks don't grow on trees though and the options are far from plentiful before the NFL trade deadline.

However, the Vikings have to explore the market. Minnesota is 6-2 and possesses one of the league's best defenses that gives the team a chance in every game. There is an argument to be made that the Vikings would be a Super Bowl frontrunner or at least a legitimate contender with average quarterback play.

More: Vikings head coach addresses quarterback conundrum after Week 9 loss

So if the Vikings can find a trade partner with a quarterback option that makes sense, they could jump at the offer – provided it doesn't break the bank. The defense deserves that much from the front office.

After all, the bar at quarterback couldn't be lower in Minnesota. Here's a look at a couple quarterback options that make sense for the Vikings on deadline day:

Vikings QB trade options

Daniel Jones, Indianapolis Colts

The Ringer's Tom Pelissero reported Sunday evening that Indy informed QB Daniel Jones before Sunday's Week 9 game they’re not trading him at the deadline. However, plans change quickly and perhaps Jones would welcome a move to a contender. And if the Colts receive an offer they can't refuse, it would be difficult to keep the quarterback.

Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner were both traded, signaling the official start of a rebuild for the Colts. And while Jones hasn't been playing at the level of someone like Kirk Cousins, an interested team like the Vikings might try to convince themselves it's a product of the situation in Indy.

Jones returned this season after a torn Achilles cut his resurgent 2025 campaign short, but it has been to less-than-stellar results. His numbers have dropped across the board, including an upside-down touchdown-to-interception ratio that includes six TDs and 10 INTs. The quarterback hasn't displayed the same level of mobility, which begs the question – what would an acquiring team be hoping for?

The Vikings do have some history with the quarterback. Jones wouldn't be walking into an unknown situation where he'd have to learn a new offense under Kevin O'Connell. Jones joined the Vikings after being released by the Giants in Nov. 2024. He stuck around on the practice squad through the end of the season before leaving in free agency to sign with the Colts.

If the Colts are willing to listen, this is one reunion that makes sense for the Vikings to explore.

More: NFL QB trade options include Kirk Cousins, Anthony Richardson and...who?

Kirk Cousins, Las Vegas Raiders

When it comes to trade candidates for the Vikings, consider this one to be the dream scenario. He is the perfect veteran option for a team that just needs someone to deliver the ball on-time to some open receivers. He can complete a screen pass and knows O'Connell's offense.

In other words, what more could you ask for?

However, ESPN's Adam Schefter reported on Nov. 8 that the Raiders hadn't received any calls for Cousins and also have no interest in trading him. After another loss, would Vegas be willing to change its stance? They should at least consider it.

The writing is on the wall in Vegas. While the Raiders are competing for a playoff spot, everyone knows Fernando Mendoza is the future for the franchise. He'll eventually take over the starting job, likely at some point this season.

It makes sense to explore a Cousins trade, given the quarterback injuries across the league. If the Raiders are taking an honest outlook this season, they'll recognize this isn't a Super Bowl-caliber team. However, there is a chance that their future Super Bowl hopes are decided by what happens at the deadline. Does trading Cousins actually hurt Mendoza's development? Losing a veteran voice as he takes over could do more harm than good.

On the other hand, Cousins might be exactly what a potential contender like Minnesota needs. Another year removed from a torn Achilles, the quarterback is playing at a high level. Maybe even high enough to book a one-way trip out of Vegas.

item.title: Klint Kubiak: We wouldn't be where we are without Kirk Cousins' "amazing" decision-making
item.description: The Raiders signed Kirk Cousins in April with the idea that he would start for the entire season while No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza develops.
item.content:encoded:
The Raiders signed Kirk Cousins in April with the idea that he would start for the entire season while No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza develops.

That plan has had solid returns, with Cousins completing 64.1 percent of his passes for 2,340 yards with 20 touchdowns and eight interceptions.

But three of those picks came in Sunday’s loss to the 49ers, which was Cousins’ worst game of the season. On Monday, head coach Klint Kubiak was asked about the QB’s decision-making on the giveaways.

“Kirk has been an extremely solid decision maker all season,” Kubiak said, via transcript from the team. “There’s ones he wants back. He wants back the first play of [the] second half. [He] wants back the one in the red zone where we did not give him protection to make a good decision. In the last play of the game, we’re trying to make a play, so he wants those back.

“But we’re not in the position that we are without the amazing decisions he’s made all year. So, we’ve got to coach up those ones and help him learn from them. But again, I’m very pleased with — the quarterback has to be the best decision-maker on the team, any organization. He wasn’t on those two plays, and that last one I’m calling a heave-ho.”

With the trade deadline rapidly approaching and the Raiders sitting at 4-5, there have been rumors about teams being interested in Cousins. Kubiak was asked how he thinks players like Cousins and Maxx Crosby — who expressed no interest in being traded — are handling that situation.

“Well, that’s the business that we’re in,” Kubiak said. “That’s the business of football, and those guys are veterans. They’ve been around that, so you just keep working. There’s a lot of things that are out of your control.”

If the Raiders were to trade Cousins, it would signal that the team feels Mendoza is ready to take over as starting quarterback. But because Las Vegas is still in the thick of things in the AFC as the current No. 9 seed, they may not be inclined to shake things up at the game’s most important position.

item.title: Saints vs. Browns: The good, the bad, and the ugly in Week 9
item.description: Saints pick up overtime win against solid Browns team
item.content:encoded:
The Good: Pass Rush

The New Orleans Saints pass rush did a great job getting to Shedeur Sanders on Sunday, sacking the second-year quarterback five times while also getting three additional tackles for loss. Carl Granderson sacked Sanders twice and Chase Young sacked him once. Both players now rank in the top 3 in the NFL in sacks with 7.5 for Granderson and 8 for Young, making them arguably the best pass rushing duo in the league so far this season. Khristian Boyd also picked up his second sack of the season, and Kaden Elliss had his best game of the year with one sack and a tackle for loss. The sacks were also very timely, with two of them coming on third down and two coming in goal to go situations which helped hold the Browns to a field goal and a turnover on downs in the red zone. The Saints run game also deserves a shoutout this week, as newly returning Audric Estime ran for 72 yards and a touchdown against the team who just waived him a week prior. Estime’s 72 yards were the most by a Saint this year, a good turnaround from their last game when Tyler Shough led the team with 7 rushing yards.

The Bad: Pass Blocking

Despite getting to Shedeur Sanders five times, the Saints also let the Browns sack Tyler Shough five times on Sunday. Four of these sacks came on third down as well, one of which probably cost the Saints three points by turning what would’ve been a 43-yard field goal into a 52-yard field goal which was missed. Only one sack came from a defensive lineman however, as the Saints struggled to keep up with the blitzes ran by Cleveland. The Browns have been good at getting to the quarterback this year, as they came into the game averaging just under 3 sacks per game, so hopefully the Saints offensive line will improve with the return of Kelvin Banks Jr. to the lineup.

The Ugly: Defensive Backs

The Saints defensive backs struggled to keep up with the Browns young receivers on Sunday. They allowed receptions of 60 yards to Denzel Boston and of 64 yards to KC Concepcion which also went for a touchdown. Concepcion beat Martin Emerson Jr. deep and was able to evade both Emerson and Julian Blackmon on his way to the end zone, and Kool-Aid McKinstry got beat deep and then was unable to find an underthrown ball leading to a 60-yard catch and run by Boston. Later in overtime Justin Reid was unable to tackle Harold Fannin Jr. in the open field which led to what could’ve been the winning touchdown if the Saints didn’t stop the ensuing two-point conversion. The Saints pass defense allowed Shedeur Sanders to have arguably the best game of his career and now ranks 28th in the NFL giving up 236 yards per game.

As Topps transitions from NFL PREM1ERE Patches to Debut Patches, previously collected memorabilia from the 2023 and 2024 rookie classes is getting a new release in 2026 Chrome Football.

The Rookie Chase Gets a Second Act

Topps is giving its retired NFL PREM1ERE Patch program another moment in the spotlight.

When 2026 Topps Chrome Football arrives November 18, collectors will have an opportunity to pursue one-of-one PREM1ERE Patch Autographs featuring material worn by players from the 2023 and 2024 NFL rookie classes during their first professional appearances.

Originally collected during the 2023 and 2024 NFL seasons, the patches are now finding their way into 2026 Topps Chrome Football. Their release comes as Topps transitions from its PREM1ERE Patch program to NFL Debut Patches, introduced for the 2026 rookie class and expected to appear in trading-card products beginning in 2027. The previously retained patches represent a retrospective addition to Chrome Football, rather than a continuation of the original program.

The checklist includes Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Puka Nacua, Jahmyr Gibbs, C.J. Stroud, Bryce Young, Drake Maye, Jayden Daniels, Caleb Williams, Bo Nix, and Brock Bowers, among others. According to Clay Luraschi, senior vice president of global product development at Fanatics Collectibles and a veteran Topps executive with more than two decades of experience shaping the company’s trading-card products, the release includes more than 100 one-of-one cards across the two classes.

This marks the second year Topps has included PREM1ERE Patch Autographs in Chrome Football. Their inclusion is positioned as a surprise-and-delight addition alongside the product’s 2026 rookie cards, Gold Shield cards, and signature short prints, introducing another premium chase without replacing the traditional rookie-card calendar.

Unlike traditional rookie cards, which can be produced in large quantities, these one-of-one autographs offer something that cannot be replicated: a piece of memorabilia tied to a player’s first NFL appearance. Beyond simply collecting a card, they offer the opportunity to own the moment itself.

Beyond the One-of-One

Sports-card manufacturers have spent decades incorporating autographs, jerseys, equipment, and other memorabilia into premium products. While scarcity remains a defining characteristic of the market, the historical significance of the material itself has become an increasingly important consideration.

A jersey swatch worn by an athlete establishes a physical connection. A patch associated with an identifiable career milestone adds context, connecting the collectible to a specific moment in sporting history.

In 2023, Topps introduced MLB Rookie Debut Patch Autographs, featuring specially created patches worn during players’ first major-league appearances and later incorporated into one-of-one autographed cards. The program established a direct relationship between a trading card and an event that occurs only once in an athlete’s career.

The NFL PREM1ERE patches commemorate a similar milestone, although their origins differ from the MLB program. Rather than being created specifically for a trading-card initiative, the NFL patches were already in the league’s possession before Topps identified an opportunity to incorporate them into its products.

“There are relic cards, and then there are relic cards that tie you to a specific moment,” Luraschi told Sam Goodman, Mantel contributor and founder of SOMOS Index.

A one-of-one designation establishes numerical rarity. The significance of a debut-worn patch comes from something more specific: its connection to the beginning of an athlete’s professional career.

The Second Life of a First Moment

When Jaxon Smith-Njigba first suited up for the Seattle Seahawks in 2023, he was a promising receiver beginning his professional career. By the time his debut-worn patch appears in 2026 Topps Chrome Football, he has led the NFL with 1,793 receiving yards, earned Offensive Player of the Year honors, and become a Super Bowl champion.

The patch hasn’t changed. The career surrounding it has.

“I think it will unlock a lot of memories for fans and collectors,” Luraschi said, pointing to Smith-Njigba as an example of how an athlete’s development can change the significance of their earliest memorabilia.

Other players offer similar examples. Brock Bowers’ debut with the Las Vegas Raiders preceded a record-setting rookie season in which he caught 112 passes for 1,194 yards. Will Anderson Jr. went on to earn Defensive Rookie of the Year honors, while Caleb Williams, the first overall selection in 2024, has since established a Chicago Bears single-season passing record and helped lead the franchise to a playoff victory.

Their careers have developed in different ways, but the patches preserve the same milestone: the beginning of an NFL career before its defining achievements were known.

“You’re getting something they wore from their first year, but you’re getting it a couple of years later,” Luraschi explained.

That separation between the year of the memorabilia and the year of the finished card is what makes the release distinctive. The PREM1ERE autographs issued in 2026 are not rookie-year cards from 2023 or 2024, but their appeal remains connected to the historical significance of those earlier seasons.

For collectors, the opportunity is no longer exclusively about projecting what a young player might accomplish. It’s also about revisiting the moments that preceded achievements they now recognize.

The 2023 and 2024 NFL PREM1ERE Collection

2023 NFL PREM1ERE

2024 NFL PREM1ERE

Owning the Moment

The transition from PREM1ERE to Debut Patches reflects a broader evolution in how manufacturers, leagues, and athletes collaborate to develop milestone-specific trading-card products.

For Fanatics, which acquired Topps in 2022, those relationships have become an important part of product innovation. Programs such as MLB Rookie Debut Patch Autographs require coordination around the creation, documentation, authentication, and eventual incorporation of memorabilia into finished cards.

Luraschi credits the leagues themselves with helping advance those concepts.

“It’s really driven the innovation in this industry,” he said. “They’re thinking about it just as much as we are.”

The earlier NFL PREM1ERE patches followed a different path into the hobby. According to Luraschi, the NFL already possessed the 2023 and 2024 patches when Topps identified an opportunity to incorporate them into its 2026 Chrome Football release.

Rather than collecting new memorabilia for another year of PREM1ERE cards, Topps is introducing previously retained artifacts into a current product as the company moves toward its Debut Patch program. The result is an additional collecting opportunity that complements the newest rookie class while giving established players another premium chase.

The strategy also extends beyond football. Luraschi said Fanatics has been developing debut-patch concepts across Formula 1, UFC, and soccer, reflecting the potential to connect trading cards with identifiable sporting milestones across different leagues.

“The idea was to be able to do this across all sports,” he said.

The secondary market has already demonstrated substantial interest in PREM1ERE Patch Autographs. In September, an unused redemption for Jaxson Dart’s one-of-one 2025 Topps Chrome Rookie PREM1ERE Patch Autograph sold for $500,200 through Goldin. According to figures provided by Fanatics, cards featuring TreVeyon Henderson and Kyle Monangai have also sold for $12,000 and $9,000, respectively.

Those transactions illustrate the premium prices that individual debut-worn cards can attract, although player popularity, performance, and collector demand remain important factors in determining their market value.

For manufacturers, the challenge is developing products that offer more than numerical scarcity. Connecting a collectible to a recognizable sporting milestone provides a different kind of significance, one rooted in the history of the athlete rather than the rarity designation alone.

“The cards have to be linked to important moments, right? Doing something just to do it is not a good idea,” Luraschi said.

As Topps moves forward with its NFL Debut Patch program, the earlier PREM1ERE memorabilia offers collectors another opportunity to revisit the beginnings of established careers.

The cards may be arriving in 2026, but the history inside them has been developing for years.

item.title: Tom Brady sells stake in Birmingham City Football Club
item.description: Tom Brady has a lot on his plate (but not any deli meat).
item.content:encoded:
Tom Brady has a lot on his plate (but not any deli meat). The man who is stretched even thinner than the most thinly-sliced slab of processed turkey has one less thing to compete for this time.

The Birmingham City Football Club has announced that Brady has exited the franchise.

"Birmingham City Football Club expresses its sincere gratitude to Tom Brady for his involvement with and unwavering support for the Club over the last three years," the team said in a website post with the headline "Tom Brady Departure."

Brady acquired a minority share in the team, and became chairman of the advisory board, in August 2023, less than a year after his second and final retirement from the NFL.

Brady, whose other gigs include serving as Fox's top NFL analyst and owning a piece of the Raiders, made waves with comments made in a Birmingham City documentary (or, as most sports documentaries now are, an infomercial) regarding the work ethic of former club manager Wayne Rooney.

There's no reason to ever question Brady's work ethic. There are plenty of reasons to question whether he tries to do too much by wearing so many hats. There are only so many hours in the day, only so many days in the week.

He has written in his newsletter (assuming he even writes it) about balance. Maybe his decision to get out of the soccer business is about achieving better balance.

If, along the way, he got a nice return on his investment, even better for Brady. Especially since he seems to be in a race with Peyton Manning to acquire enough money to become the controlling owner of an NFL team.

The biggest problem is this. As Brady's net worth grows, the price tag for NFL ownership grows even faster.

Regardless, he likely now has more cash to add to the fund for potentially purchasing a franchise and, more importantly, one less thing to consume his time and attention.

item.title: Week 10 NFL Power Rankings: Did the 49ers move up after big win over Raiders?
item.description: The Niners had a huge win on Sunday. Did it change their standing in the power rankings?
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers blew past the Las Vegas Raiders 38-17 on Sunday, taking advantage of the opposing defense while forcing five turnovers in a dominant win.

It was a good all-around performance for the 49ers, who remain tied for the NFL’s best record at 7-1 with the Buffalo Bills.

After their big win on Sunday, where do the 49ers rank in the Week 10 NFL Power Rankings?

ESPN: No. 2

The 49ers stayed at No. 2 behind the Buffalo Bills in ESPN’s weekly power rankings, which makes sense given that Buffalo beat the Minnesota Vikings on Monday Night Football in a battle of one-loss teams.

The top three included the Jacksonville Jaguars last week. That remained the same this week, while the Chicago Bears climbed up one spot to No. 4 and the Denver Broncos fell one spot to No. 5 despite both teams winning. The rest of the Top 10 remained the same, just in a different order.

The Kansas City Chiefs stayed put at No. 6. The Cincinnati Bengals bumped up from No. 10 to No. 7 after a 34-17 win over the Atlanta Falcons. The Vikings fell one spot following their loss to the Bills, landing at No. 8. The Seattle Seahawks actually fell one spot to No. 9 after beating the Arizona Cardinals 17-3. And the Detroit Lions also fell one spot to No. 10 after beating the Miami Dolphins.

Looking ahead at the rest of the schedule, ESPN believes Week 12 against the Seattle Seahawks is the most important game left on the docket.

The Athletic: No. 2

Just like the previous ranking, the 49ers stay at No. 2 here again behind the Buffalo Bills, earning a midseason grade of an ‘A’.

“The Niners have the second-best point differential in the NFL (plus-79), and they hardly broke a sweat Sunday in another multi-touchdown game from Christian McCaffrey,” The Athletic’s Chad Graff and Josh Kendall wrote. “His 37 career touchdown receptions are the most by a running back in the Super Bowl era, surpassing Marshall Faulk.”

The Broncos remained at No. 3 here, while the Chiefs moved up one spot to No. 4 and the Jaguars moved up one spot to No. 5. Wrapping up the top 10 were the Bears (No. 6), Bengals (No. 7), Lions (No. 8), Packers (No. 9), and Vikings (No. 10).

CBS Sports: No. 2

CBS Sports’s Pete Prisco’s rankings did not see a change inside the top five, meaning the 49ers stayed at No. 2 behind the Bills.

“They just keep playing as well as anybody in the NFC, despite their many injuries,” Prisco wrote. “Brock Purdy is in the MVP talk.”

The Bills, 49ers, Jaguars, Bears, and Broncos remained the top five here, while the Chiefs, Bengals, Lions, Steelers, and Packers rounded out the top 10. Each of those teams moved up one spot, while the Vikings dropped five to No. 11.

FOX Sports: No. 3

The 49ers stayed the same as last week here, only that was at No. 3 behind the Bills and the Broncos.

“The 49ers clearly fixed whatever it was that happened to them before the bye week when they lost to the Falcons — a game that now looks like a weird blip on their otherwise stellar season,” FOX Sports’s Ralph Vacchiano wrote. “They came out strong and fast, putting the Las Vegas Raiders in their place quickly.

“And the fact that they did it without WR Mike Evans made it even more impressive. Of course, that’s what they do best: Overcome injuries. They’re that good and they’re that deep. They still look like they deserve to be the NFC favorites. And they’re clearly the NFC’s best team.”

Behind the 49ers were the Chiefs and Bears, who were in the top five last week. Then came the Jaguars, Vikings, Bengals, Packers, and Lions, with Green Bay making a big jump from No. 15 to No. 9.

item.title: How the Giants Dennard Wilson, Arvell Reese destroyed the Eagles’ passing attack
item.description: Arvell Reese is exceptional and Dennard Wilson understands how to maximize his potential.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants have one of the NFL’s most promising young coaches in Dennard Wilson, who is finding ways to maximize the immense young talent on the roster. Rookie linebacker Arvell Reese credited the coaching staff’s strategic use of him as a key factor in his success. Reese had 1.5 sacks and six pressures heading into the Giants’ Week 9 matchup against the Philadelphia Eagles.

The Giants traded Dexter Lawrence during the offseason, leaving a significant void in their ability to generate interior pressure. Lawrence had been a consistent force disrupting quarterbacks from the inside, but Wilson has found another way to manufacture pressure through creative blitz packages that attack the interior. He recognizes Reese’s ability as a pass rusher and the mismatch he creates when matched up against running backs in pass protection.

New York deployed a variety of pressure looks aimed at the center and guards, with defensive linemen widening their rush paths to manipulate the protection. Players like Kayvon Thibodeaux (5) would feign an outside rush, forcing offensive linemen to account for them as potential threats. This approach occupies blockers and creates advantageous one-on-one matchups elsewhere along the line — opportunities that a versatile talent like Arvell Reese can exploit.

The hit heard around the world

Charlie Jones fumbled a punt giving the Eagles the ball in Giants’ territory with all the momentum in the world; a situation that would have crippled past Giants’ teams. However, New York forced a third-and-5 pass attempt where Joe Milton was hit hard Reese:

New York schemed three over two to the offensive left side (where Reese was); Dawuane Smoot (96) aligned as a 4i-shade, with Thibodeaux wide of the tackle and Reese wide of Thibodeaux. Micah McFadden (41) sugared the A-Gap, forcing center attention, with Darius Alexander as a three-technique (91), Abdul Carter (3) as a five-technique, and Dru Phillips (22) wide of Carter.

The loaded line of scrimmage led to Saquon Barkley (26) accounting for McFadden and the three other rushers to the offensive right – and NO ONE accounted for Reese the left, including Milton. Both Smoot and Alexander dropped off into coverage, with Thibodeaux acting effectively as a spy once his initial rush was stopped and the four-man rush got home for an unblocked sack-forced fumble. Here’s another video of the hit:

Reese’s second sack

via GIPHY

Reese had another third-down sack, this time on third-and-10. Wilson overloaded the offensive right side with four players on the line of scrimmage: Thibodeaux, Smoot, Alexander, and Tae Banks (2); Wilson aggressively aligns the corners in press coverage versus condensed fronts to gain a numbers advantage in the pass rush — Wilson isn’t shy about sending the cornerback to creatively cover the receiver.

Reese is stacked behind Alexander, and he slants opposite to the protection slide toward McFadden and Carter, who both have one-on-one matchups due to the pressure-look. Elijah Mitchell (39) did an excellent job picking up McFadden, and Reese was stopped by the guard, so he slid off the rush and eyed Milton, who attempted to run into green grass, but instead found the waiting arms of an elite Ohio State rookie linebacker.

Reese’s third sack

via GIPHY

Reese’s third sack came on third-and-10 with 7:22 left in the fourth quarter. Reese was aligned off the line of scrimmage in a 4i-shade with Thibodeaux to his right, wide of the tackle. Alexander was over the center, which isolated Reese against the guard, Landon Dickerson (69). New York ran a game with Reese penetrating the B-Gap for Thibodeaux to undercut and loop into the A-Gap, while another twist happened with Alexander and Carter.

Final thoughts

Wilson is on a tear. He’s generating pressure in a variety of different ways with a lot of exotic coverage looks on the back-end. Wilson uses disguise on a loaded line of scrimmage, while dropping his short-zone coverages off the line of scrimmage after declaring a rush, which effectively wastes blockers and isolates players like Reese and Abdul Carter into valuable one-on-one matchups.

Not only do the Giants have immensely talented young defensive players, but the coach understands how to best maximize the talent. Arvell Reese is now the favorite to win defensive rookie of the year, but conversations about defensive player of the year are starting to happen. With performances like Week 9, it’s not crazy to mention his name in that conversation.

item.title: A Vikings-Matthew Stafford trade transforms them into a Super Bowl contender
item.description: James Dator has a blockbuster trade proposal that would reshape the NFL.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL trade deadline is looming and there’s clearly one contender in need of an upgrade that could turn them into one of the scariest teams in the NFC. The Minnesota Vikings should go all-in on trading for Matthew Stafford, and they should do itnow.

On Monday night, we witnessed the Vikings dictate the tempo for much of the game against the Bills with their staggering defense. It frustrated Josh Allen, transforming one of the league’s best QBs into any other guy. The hard work was squandered, because Minnesota simply couldn’t do anything on offense, shackled to the bum arm of Carson Wentz, who couldn’t even make the simplest downfield throws that could have given them an advantage. Eventually the dam broke, and the Bills ran away with the game.

Wentz’s final numbers were some of the most putrid we’ve seen in a primetime game this season: 8-for-25, 81 passing yards, 2 interceptions. It was an extension of the quarterback issues we’ve seen play out this season for the Vikings, lost in an endless sea of ineptitude under center while the defense continues to play lights-out football, dragging the offense to wins, kicking and screaming.

Another thing happened on Monday that will transform the playoff picture. The Rams announced that star wide receiver Puka Nacua would be placed on IR after spraining his MCL and PCL in the team’s win over the Commanders. Los Angeles’ season is effectively over with Nacua out, and Davante Adams still recovering from a ruptured hamstring. It’s been a series of bad breaks and ugly performances for the Rams in a season that once held so much promise.

Sean McVay has a decision to make: Does he keep trying to chase down the 49ers, or does he punt on the rest of the season and try to prepare for 2027? Looking at the Rams’ schedule, there is one correct option, and it’s pulling the Band-Aid off. After they face the Cardinals in Week 10, Los Angeles is set to face the Packers, Chiefs, 49ers, Cowboys, and Seahawks. Without their top receiving weapons the Rams would likely lose four of these games, and could very well struggle against the Cowboys as well, especially if the game becomes an offensive shootout. That would put the team at 7-8 or 8-7, with either record meaning Los Angeles is likely to miss the playoffs.

Alternatively, the team could prep for the future. They selected Alabama quarterback Ty Simpson with the 13th pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, and getting him some live-fire reps could put the team in a much better position down the road. It would also be an incredibly kind move to Matthew Stafford, the reigning MVP who has done everything for the Rams since arriving in 2021. Stafford put his body on the line, played through pain, and might only have one last shot at getting another ring.

To this end, Minnesota isn’t just a potential landing spot; it’s an incredible landing spot for Stafford. With the Vikings he would be reunited with Kevin O’Connell, who served as his offensive coordinator on the 2021 Super Bowl team. Minnesota functionally runs the Sean McVay variant of the West Coast offense, and offensive coordinator Wes Phillips served as the passing game coordinator for the Rams on the same 2021 Super Bowl team. Stafford would functionally be walking into the same system he’s running right now, albeit with Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, and T.J. Hockenson to catch the ball.

Those two receivers are critical to why this would be a runaway success, because they only need someone with an arm who can target them downfield. Minnesota is one of the worst teams in the NFL when it comes to yards-per-reception, as well as only 39 passes of 20+ yards, languishing near the bottom of the league. That is inexcusable when an offense has Jefferson and Addison, and it’s purely because of their QB position.

Stafford would be able to walk in immediately and stretch the field. With the threat of explosive throws looming, teams could no longer stack the box to stop the run game. Just getting one guy who can accurately throw downfield would be so transformative to the offense that when paired with an already stellar defense, well, the Vikings could become the favorite in the NFC overnight.

Moreover, there’s a 2027 trigger point in Stafford’s contract where he could easily be released without much of a cap ramification for the Vikings, allowing him to potentially turn around and re-sign back with the Rams to close out his career when they are able to compete again — or, simple sail off into the sunset being the legend who finally helped bring the Vikings a Super Bowl ring, if they should be. so lucky.

If there’s one trade that should happen this year it’s this one. The Vikings should be blowing up the Rams’ phone as we speak to try and make a deal, then the NFL can reel from its cataclysmic aftermath.
